source.title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
source.authors: T. Bolukbasi; Adam Pearce; Ann Yuan; A. Coenen; Emily Reif; Fernanda Vi'egas; M. Wattenberg

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that neuron interpretations based on top-activating sentences change across datasets, challenging the idea that such examples establish a stable, general interpretation.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results about dataset separability, token monotonicity, local coherence, and annotator agreement. Results not measuring the cross-dataset consistency of neuron interpretations or the pattern evidence used to motivate it are not included as rows. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Human annotators found patterns in each dataset's top-activating sentences, but these did not carry across datasets (about 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron over four datasets). This is direct evidence that an explanation fitting activating examples can fail to predict where the unit fires, which is V6. It is not one of V6's original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors also state that the illusion is equally pervasive for random directions as for neurons, and that it likely occurs in earlier layers (informal check of layers 2 and 7). They also note that global directions, such as those for pronouns and common verbs, do exist.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses human annotation of top-activating sentence sets across four datasets, rather than testing explanations by predicting neuron activations on new text.
record.method_sensitivity: The patterns found for top-activating sentences vary by dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Random directions showed patterns in their top-activating sentences as often as basis neurons did (82% vs 80%). The authors say the illusion is equally pervasive among neurons and random directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In BERT's final [CLS] embedding, individual neuron axes are no more interpretable from top-activating examples than random directions, i.e. there is no privileged basis.

record.problems: The study relies on human judgments of patterns, reports annotator disagreement and differences in annotators' tendency to find patterns, and does not directly score explanation predictions on held-out activations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows retained. The paper's other quantitative analyses concern dataset separation, token monotonicity, local-coherence scores, or annotator variation rather than directly measuring the cross-dataset consistency of neuron interpretations or held-out predictive accuracy.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or share of neuron poles with one, two or unknown jobs.
No comparison across model families, MoE models or scale; BERT-base only.
No InceptionV1 or cat-and-car analysis, and no recursive-generalization account.
No architecture, regularization or tool comparisons.
No attribution graphs or replacement models.

No written explanation is scored quantitatively on held-out activations. Only final-layer [CLS] residual dimensions of BERT-base were examined, not MLP neurons or large modern LMs. Earlier layers were looked at only informally.

missing.what: Random-direction condition: 27/33 (82%) of sets judged patterned, versus neurons at 20/25 (80%) and random sentence sets at 4/29 (14%), with annotator split rates of 18%, 8% and 38%.

Neuron/token monotonicity across quintiles. Over a quarter of pairs are monotonic within single datasets, but only about 0.8–1.9% across all four datasets, against a 1.7% chance rate. This is the cross-dataset consistency of direction meaning.
Locality scores: meaningful directions score higher than meaningless ones (0.026 vs 0.010, p=0.0004). This indicates the annotated patterns arise from local embedding geometry.

record.verdict_notes: The 'neurons' here are basis dimensions of BERT's final-layer [CLS] hidden state (residual output), not MLP neurons, and they are evaluated on sentence-level embeddings. The sample is small: 25 neurons, each set annotated by two people, with annotator rates of finding patterns ranging from 0.56 to 1.6 per direction. The study tests V6 qualitatively through cross-dataset inconsistency rather than through quantitative prediction scoring.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit shares, neuron poles, and percentages are not measured. The study examines BERT-base uncased using a different procedure.
No sweep across model families, dense or mixture-of-experts architectures, or model scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, or recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of architectures, regularization, tools, or interpretability estimates across vision models.
No attribution graphs or comparison of neuron-based explanations with a trained replacement model.

The study compares top-activating examples and their human-annotated patterns across datasets; it does not test a written explanation's predictions on separately collected activations or quantify prediction accuracy.
No automated scoring of explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: BERT-base uncased
rows.operation_detail: Annotators assessed whether sets of top-activating sentences showed a pattern

conditions.value: QQP, QNLI, Wiki, and Books; aggregate

rows.measure: Share of top-activating sentence sets judged to contain at least one pattern
rows.baseline: 14% of randomly drawn sentence sets contained patterns
rows.value: more than 80% of top activating sentences contained patterns
rows.note: The paper reports this as an aggregate across the four datasets. Pattern presence in the examples is not itself a test of whether an interpretation predicts activations on new text.
rows.check: This row shows that top-activating sets look patterned (neurons 20/25, 80%, vs 14% for random sentence sets). That is V6's premise, not its effect, so 'partial' is wrong. The record also omits that random directions scored 82%, the same as neurons.

source_check.correct: Neurons, all datasets: both annotators found a pattern in 20 of 25 sets (80%); 3 (12%) no, 2 (8%) conflicting. The text's 'more than 80%' isn't split by direction type; random directions were 27/33 (82%). Baseline: random sentence sets 4/29 (14%).

source_check.problem: Row is tied to directions=neurons, but the neuron cell is exactly 80% (20/25), not 'more than 80%'. cannot_determine is still right because pattern presence is V6's premise.

rows.subject: BERT-base uncased
rows.operation_detail: Compared patterns annotators found for each neuron across four datasets
rows.measure: Mean number of distinct annotated patterns per neuron across datasets
rows.value: 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron on average
rows.note: The authors report that interpretations changed substantially with the dataset used to find top-activating sentences.
rows.check: Correct as a V6 result. The subject is 25 randomly chosen basis dimensions of the final-layer [CLS] hidden state, not MLP neurons. The natural ceiling is 4 patterns, one per dataset; no baseline is stated.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, text before Figure 2: 'on average 2.5 distinct patterns across QQP, QNLI, Wiki, and Books'
source_check.problem: Fine. The subject is randomly chosen final-layer [CLS] basis dimensions, not MLP neurons. The value is a text-stated average; no baseline is given; the ceiling is 4.

rows.subject: BERT-base uncased
rows.operation_detail: Compared ranges of the top ten activation values across dataset pairs and neurons

conditions.value: QQP, QNLI, Wiki, and Books; all dataset pairs and neurons

rows.measure: Share of activation ranges that overlapped
rows.value: 38% of the ranges of the top 10 activations overlap
rows.note: This is an overlap result across datasets, not a direct score of an explanation's ability to predict activations.
rows.check: The 38% overlap of top-10 activation ranges is the authors' mechanism for the illusion (datasets occupy distinct regions). It is not a measure of whether interpretations fail, so it cannot show V6's effect; 'partial' is not meaningful here.

relationships.condition: BERT-base uncased, 25 final-layer [CLS] basis dimensions, top-10 sentences from QQP, QNLI, Wiki and Books, two human annotators
relationships.reason: Patterns inferred from one dataset's top examples did not hold on others, averaging 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron across four datasets (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Patterns inferred from one dataset's top examples did not carry over to the others, with an average of 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron across the four datasets.

relation.reason: Its own results on whether top-example interpretations stay consistent across datasets bear directly on V6.

tranche.reason: The paper argues that interpretations from top-activating examples do not generalize across datasets, so readings of a unit by inspection need restating. It uses human annotation rather than a prediction test.

source_check.notes: Units are random basis dimensions of the final-layer [CLS] embedding. Rebuilt from the garbled layout, Table 1's per-dataset neuron counts (8/6/5/6) sum to 25, so '25 neurons' may count neuron-dataset sets. The illusion holds equally for random directions; layers 2 and 7 were checked only informally; global directions (pronouns, common verbs) exist.

statements.problem: The BERT part is right: 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron on average across QQP, QNLI, Wiki and Books, from annotators reading each dataset's top-10 sentences. Other studies were not checked.

statements.correction: In sets judged meaningful, patterns covered a mean of 6.80 of the 10 top sentences for neurons (SD 2.37), 6.89 for random directions and 5.05 for random sentence sets. A pattern needed at least 3 examples (Figure 2, bottom).
statements.problem: 20/25 neuron sets (80%) against 4/29 random sets (14%) is right. But the claim that pattern presence is the nearest measure of fit to source examples leaves out that this study also counts how many of the top 10 sentences fit the pattern.
Right: units are basis dimensions of BERT-base uncased's final-layer [CLS] hidden state, which the paper calls neurons. They are not MLP neurons.
Right: the annotated patterns depend on which dataset the top sentences come from, with 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron on average across four datasets.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: BERT-base uncased, neurons examined using QQP, QNLI, Wiki, and Books
reader_labels.reason: The same neurons yielded an average of 2.5 distinct patterns across datasets, and the top-activation ranges overlapped only in the reported 38% of comparisons; these results support caution about treating patterns in activating examples as stable explanations (r2, r3).
